newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - Making promises with fingers crossed.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Making promises with fingers crossed.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard has in the past two days significantly disowned responsibility for political promises.
On Monday he refused to accept that the government would be bound by a shadow minister's pre-election commitment.
Today he has declined to accept responsibility for a statement issued in his own name but prepared by someone else.
This seems to drastically reduce the status of anything said in an election campaign -- and perhaps at other times -- unless it was uttered personally by Howard himself.
Howard on Sunday announced a work-for-the-dole scheme for some young people in some regional areas. He said he had never ruled out such a scheme while in opposition.

But opposition industry spokesman Simon Crean on Monday confronted Howard with the fact that in 1995 the then Liberal-National opposition, through its then employment spokesmen David Kemp, had said there was no such proposal.
Howard responded: "That press release that you referred to was not issued by me and therefore the statement that I made was true, the statement I made yesterday was absolutely true."

Today Howard began Question Time by partially correcting his Sunday statement. Words attributed to him in a newspaper during the election campaign had rejected work-for-the-dole but they were really not his words, he said.
"The response to the (newspaper) question was not brought to my attention or the attention of my staff before it was submitted and it was published in my name on page 21 of the Melbourne Herald-Sun."
This seems to leave the opposition with enormous opportunities.
Next time a government minister makes some assurance, surely the opposition can say: "It doesn't mean a thing until Howard confirms it."
Next time something is published in Howard's name, it could say: "It doesn't mean a thing until we hear it from his own mouth."
All of this is novel. Politics has always worked on the assumption that if you commit to something you are taken at your word and if you do not do it (as often happens) you cop the criticism.
Howard's denial of responsibility for the coalition's statements also seems quite at odds with his own very strong emphasis on high standards of political ethics.
That too gives the opposition more ammunition.
